title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Los Angeles, CA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Los Angeles welders, QC staff and inspectors: online study or on-site groups, plus LADBS, port and seismic steel context.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Los Angeles: A Six-Day Course for Welders and Inspectors
html:
Los Angeles produces more kinds of welding inspection than most American cities. There is wharf and crane steel at the ports, seismic moment frames in office towers and hospitals, aerospace hardware in the South Bay, refinery piping along the coast, and transit and bridge work that rarely pauses. This page explains how the six-day AWS Certified Welding Inspector exam-preparation course from Atlantis NDT fits a candidate or an employer in that market. The course is built for welders, fitters, quality-control staff, NDT technicians and engineers who intend to sit the AWS CWI examination. A single candidate works online through a structured plan, with course materials, practice questions written for the course and an instructor on hand for questions. A company that wants several people prepared together can book the full six days at its own plant, yard or office instead. To scope either option, ask for a Los Angeles quote.

One point needs to be clear before anything else, because it shapes every decision that follows. The American Welding Society (AWS) runs every part of the CWI exam and is the body that grants the credential. Atlantis's job stops at preparation: it certifies nobody, never writes or sees an exam paper, and AWS has neither approved nor endorsed the course. You apply to AWS yourself, you meet its education and experience rules, and you pass its vision examination on your own. The practice questions are Atlantis originals, drafted against the topics AWS publishes for the exam, and not one of them comes from a real AWS paper.

Where welding inspection work comes from in Los Angeles

The San Pedro Bay port complex, with the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach side by side, is the obvious starting point. Container cranes, wharf structures, terminal buildings, pile-supported decks and the rail yards behind them are welded steel, and they are rebuilt and extended in phases rather than all at once. Much of that work is structural welding under AWS D1.1. It needs inspectors who can check fit-up, preheat, procedure compliance and finished weld profiles on steel that will spend its life in salt air, where a poor weld toe or an undercut groove becomes a corrosion site within a few seasons.

Buildings are the second source, and in Los Angeles they come with seismic history. The 1994 Northridge earthquake exposed brittle fractures in welded steel moment-frame connections, and the research that followed reshaped how those connections are designed, welded and inspected. Seismic welding requirements now sit in their own AWS document, D1.8, the structural welding code seismic supplement. A structural engineer in Los Angeles is likely to specify it alongside D1.1 for the lateral system of a steel building. A welding inspector on such a job reads both codes, the structural drawings and the special inspection program written for the project.

Aerospace and space hardware is the third source. The South Bay, Long Beach and the Antelope Valley host aircraft, satellite and launch-vehicle manufacturing, supported by a deep tier of machine shops and weld shops. Fusion welding on flight hardware is usually done to AWS D17.1 or to a customer specification, and the quality systems in those plants expect inspection records that trace back to an individual part, joint and welder.

Refining is the fourth. Refineries in El Segundo, Torrance, Wilmington and Carson run maintenance and turnaround work on pressure piping, vessels, exchangers and tanks. Piping repairs there are typically built to ASME B31.3, with welding procedures qualified to ASME Section IX by the owner or the contractor. Add transit construction, freeway interchanges, water and power utilities, and a large manufacturing base in the San Gabriel Valley and the Inland Empire, and the region produces steady demand for people who can judge a weld against a written standard and defend that judgment on paper.

LADBS rules a Los Angeles CWI should understand

Inside the City of Los Angeles, the Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) sets its own rules for who may inspect and who may weld on structural work, and new CWIs are often surprised by them. LADBS registers deputy inspectors by category. Welding falls under its Steel Construction category, which covers structural steel, welding, high-strength bolting, cold-formed steel framing and pile foundations. The department's 2023 bulletin on deputy inspector registration asks applicants in that category to hold current ICC certifications in structural steel and bolting and in structural welding, to have a high school diploma or equivalent, to document related work experience, and to pass an LADBS written examination followed by an oral interview. That bulletin does not name the AWS CWI as the qualifying credential.

This matters for career planning. The CWI is widely accepted for welding inspection under AWS D1.1, and many employers across the region ask for it, yet on its own it does not make you an LADBS registered deputy inspector. People who want deputy work inside the city usually hold the CWI and the two ICC certifications, then register with LADBS. The CWI preparation still pays off on that route, because the LADBS reference list for Steel Construction is built around AWS codes: the city-adopted editions of D1.1, D1.3 for sheet steel, D1.4 for reinforcing steel and D1.8 for seismic work, plus the AISC steel construction manual.

Watch the editions. The bulletin lists the city-adopted D1.1-2015, while AWS uses the 2020 edition of D1.1 for Part C of the CWI exam. Clause numbering changed between those two editions, so a candidate who learns to move quickly through the 2020 book for the exam should also practise finding the same requirements in the 2015 book if city deputy work is the goal.

LADBS also certifies welders. Under the Los Angeles Building Code, welders doing structural work must be qualified to AWS requirements and certified by the department, except when the welding happens in the shop of an approved fabricator. The welder takes a written department examination and then a performance test in each classification and process applied for, and a testing agency approved by the department monitors that test and reports the result. Certificates are issued for three years. A welder who goes six continuous months without welding in a classification has to test again. The agencies that monitor those tests, inspect field welds and report to the building department are among the most common employers of welding inspectors in the city.

Who hires CWIs around Los Angeles

  • Testing and inspection agencies. They staff special and deputy inspection on building projects, monitor welder performance tests and supply inspectors to public works. A CWI is a common entry requirement for their welding staff, usually alongside the ICC structural certifications.
  • Structural steel fabricators and erectors. Shops supplying high-rise, hospital, school and warehouse projects keep welding inspectors on their quality staff to check procedure compliance, welder qualification records and finished welds before steel leaves the yard. A shop that welds under an approved-fabricator arrangement carries more of the inspection burden itself, so its in-house records have to stand up to review.
  • Port, terminal and marine contractors. Crane rail, wharf steel, mooring hardware and terminal structures need inspection during fabrication and erection, often on night shifts around vessel schedules.
  • Aerospace suppliers. Weld shops working to D17.1 or to a prime contractor's specification employ inspectors who understand weld classes, acceptance criteria and traceable records.
  • Refinery owners and their contractors. Piping and vessel repairs during maintenance and turnarounds need welding inspection against B31.3 and the site's own engineering standards.
  • Public agencies and their consultants. Transit, bridge, water and power projects write welding inspection into their contract specifications, and those specifications often name the CWI as the minimum.

Where Los Angeles candidates take the AWS exam

The CWI examination has three parts. Part A, Fundamentals, has 150 questions on welding processes, metallurgy, destructive and nondestructive testing, welding symbols, procedure documents, safety and the arithmetic an inspector uses. Part B, Practical, has 46 questions built around hands-on tasks: using inspection tools on samples and applying welding procedure and qualification documents. Part C is an open-book test of 50 to 65 questions on the code book you choose. AWS currently requires a minimum of 72 percent on each part.

AWS delivers Parts A and C as computer-based tests at Prometric centres, and it states there are more than 100 of those in the United States. Part B is not given at Prometric; AWS holds it at its seminar locations. Los Angeles and Sacramento are both on the current AWS list of US CWI seminar cities, so a candidate from the basin does not need to leave California for the practical. Prometric scheduling needs the eligibility code from the AWS confirmation letter, which fixes the order of events: the application is accepted by AWS first, then you book. Dates at both Prometric and the seminar sites move through the year, so confirm them on aws.org before you plan time off.

Choosing a Part C code book for Los Angeles work

AWS currently lets candidates choose among AWS D1.1 (2020), API 1104 (22nd edition), AWS D1.2 (2014) for aluminum, AWS D1.5 (2020) for bridges, AWS D15.1 (2019) for railroad cars and locomotives, AWS D17.1 (2024) for aerospace, ASME Section IX, ASME B31.1 and ASME B31.3, among others. Part C rewards speed and familiarity in one book, so the sensible choice is the code you will actually work to after you pass.

Los Angeles workPart C book to considerWhy
Building steel, special inspection, port and terminal structuresAWS D1.1The base structural code on most steel jobs in the city; LADBS references it too
Freeway, transit and bridge structuresAWS D1.5Bridge fabrication has its own welding code with stricter controls on fracture-critical members
Aircraft, satellite and launch-vehicle fabricationAWS D17.1The fusion welding specification used across aerospace work
Refinery and process pipingASME B31.3The process piping code behind most refinery repairs and tie-ins
Aluminum structures and marine fabricationsAWS D1.2Aluminum behaves differently in welding and has its own structural code

Note what is missing from the list. D1.8, the seismic supplement, is not a Part C option even though it appears on many Los Angeles steel projects. A candidate aiming at building work should take Part C in D1.1, then study D1.8 once certified, paying attention to demand-critical welds and the extra controls the supplement places on them. For an overview of how D1.1 acceptance works, see the D1.1 acceptance criteria guide and the AWS D1.1 standard summary.

How the six days work for a Los Angeles candidate or employer

The outline is the same whether you study alone or with colleagues, and the full day-by-day plan is on the national AWS CWI exam prep course page. In short: two days of fundamentals (processes, joint design, the weld and welding symbols drawn in AWS A2.4, the vocabulary defined in AWS A3.0, metallurgy, mechanical testing, discontinuities, safety and inspector duties), one day on the practical skills behind Part B, one day learning to navigate your chosen code book for Part C, one day of timed practice exams for all three parts with review, and a final day on weak areas, exam-day strategy and the application checklist.

Individuals work through that plan online at their own pace, with materials, original practice questions and an instructor who answers questions as they come up. That suits a welder on a port project or a refinery shift who cannot step away for a block of days. There are no fixed start dates and no scheduled online classes; you start when you enrol and spread the six days of content over the weeks you have.

Employers can bring the whole six-day programme onto their own premises for a group of staff. For a Los Angeles fabricator, testing agency or aerospace weld shop, that has a practical advantage on the third day: the group practises measuring and gauging with the company's own fillet gauges, undercut gauges, calipers and weld samples, on joints like the ones it builds every week. Atlantis does not ship replica kits; the practical work uses what the employer has on hand. Atlantis has no classroom in Los Angeles, so on-site delivery means your premises, and it is the only in-person format offered.

Two free tools help between study sessions. The NDT practice tests sharpen the testing and discontinuity questions in Part A, and the welding workshop scenario in Practical NDT lets a candidate rehearse inspection routines on screen. For realistic expectations by exam part, read the CWI pass rate breakdown by part.

Meeting AWS eligibility from Los Angeles

AWS sets eligibility in QC1, its specification for the certification of welding inspectors; the edition it lists today is QC1:2016 with Amendment 1. The rule trades formal education against years of welding-based work experience:

Highest educationWelding-based experience AWS expects
Welding engineering or welding engineering technology, bachelor's level or aboveAt least one year
Associate degree or higher in welding, an engineering technology, engineering or physical scienceAt least two years
Engineering or technical courses that count toward a welding bachelor's degreeAt least three years
Completed trade or vocational coursesAt least four years
High school diploma or an approved equivalentAt least five years
Eighth-grade schoolingAt least nine years
Less than eighth gradeAt least twelve years

AWS also asks for an employment verification form covering the experience you claim, a vision examination recorded on its Visual Acuity Exam Form, and acceptable photo identification. AWS decides what counts as welding-based work, so describe your duties plainly: welding, fitting, welding supervision, quality control, or inspection of welded construction. The sixth day of the course walks through that paperwork, but completing it and passing the vision examination remain the candidate's own steps. For a fuller explanation of the requirements, see CWI certification requirements and career impact.

Welding schools and AWS sections around Los Angeles

AWS organizes its members into local sections, and the Los Angeles basin has three of them within AWS District 21: Los Angeles/Inland Empire, Long Beach/Orange County and San Fernando Valley. Section meetings are where inspectors, fabricators, educators and suppliers in the area meet. They are a practical way to find a mentor, hear about inspection openings and ask which local employers sponsor candidates. Ask your section how its technical meetings relate to AWS professional development hours, which become important when recertification comes around.

On the welding side, community colleges across Los Angeles County run welding programs that feed both the trade and, years later, the inspection workforce. College of the Canyons in Santa Clarita is one example; its welding department publishes the LADBS welder certification rules for students, which shows how closely local training tracks the city's requirements. A welder who comes up through a program like that, earns LADBS welder certification and then builds several years of structural work has exactly the experience profile AWS looks for on a CWI application.

After the exam: renewal, recertification and next steps

AWS runs the CWI on a nine-year cycle. Renewal falls due at the third and sixth years, and to renew you confirm that you have had no break in practice or employment longer than two years within the previous three. At the end of nine years you recertify, for example by passing Part B again or by logging 80 professional development hours, or by another route AWS lists. A Certified Associate Welding Inspector (CAWI) can later upgrade to CWI, and experienced CWIs can work toward Senior CWI, described in the SCWI pathway article.

Many Los Angeles inspectors add NDT methods to the CWI because building, port and refinery specifications often call for magnetic particle or ultrasonic examination of the same welds. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, under which your employer certifies you to its written practice; a course alone certifies no one. Visual testing is the natural first step: see VT Level 1 and VT Level 2, or the NDT training options for Los Angeles. API 510, 570 and 653 preparation sits outside what Atlantis teaches. If you are comparing the CWI with an NDT or API credential, read AWS CWI vs API 577 vs ASNT Level II. For field work rather than training, Atlantis provides weld inspection services in Los Angeles and visual testing in Los Angeles.

Getting a quote for Los Angeles

Send a short note covering whether this is for one person or a group, how many candidates and what they do now, their years of welding-based experience, the Part C code book they plan to use, and the exam window they are aiming for. For an on-site group, add the site address and whether you have a quiet room, gauges and weld samples the group can use. Current AWS exam and seminar charges are posted on aws.org; to plan the whole budget, use the CWI exam budget planner. Request the Los Angeles quote here; we reply within one business day.

Candidates elsewhere in the West can read the San Diego CWI page, the Phoenix version for Arizona fab and data-centre work or the Portland, Oregon page.

faq.q: Is an AWS CWI enough to work as an LADBS deputy inspector in Los Angeles?
faq.a: Not by itself. The LADBS 2023 registration bulletin puts welding under the Steel Construction category and asks for current ICC structural steel and bolting and structural welding certifications, documented experience, and an LADBS written exam plus oral interview. Many deputy inspectors hold the CWI as well, because the city's reference list is built on AWS codes.

faq.q: Can I take the CWI practical exam in Los Angeles?
faq.a: AWS currently lists Los Angeles, and Sacramento, among its US CWI seminar locations, which is where Part B is given. Parts A and C are taken at a Prometric centre. Confirm dates on aws.org, because the schedule changes during the year.

faq.q: Which Part C code book suits building work in Los Angeles?
faq.a: AWS D1.1 for most structural steel. D1.8, the seismic supplement many local engineers specify, is not offered for Part C, so study it after you pass. Bridge candidates may prefer D1.5, aerospace candidates D17.1, and refinery candidates ASME B31.3.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run a CWI classroom in Los Angeles?
faq.a: No. Solo candidates prepare online and send their questions to an instructor; a company with several candidates books the programme at its own site. Atlantis keeps no classroom or office anywhere in Los Angeles.
The content is six days. Employer groups usually take it as six consecutive days on site; individuals online work through the same six days of material at a pace that fits their shifts.

faq.q: Are the practice questions taken from the real AWS exam?
faq.a: No. Atlantis writes original questions to the published body of knowledge. Real AWS examination questions are confidential, and the course never uses them.

faq.q: Will finishing the course make me a CWI?
faq.a: No. AWS administers the examination and issues the certification. You must meet AWS education and experience rules, pass its vision examination and pass all three parts of the exam.

faq.q: Can our fabrication shop or testing agency host the course?
faq.a: Yes. The six days can be delivered at your premises for your staff, and the practical day can use your own gauges and weld samples. Send group size, roles and site address through the quote form; we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Where can I see what the AWS exam will cost me?
faq.a: The application, exam and seminar charges are set by AWS and listed on aws.org. The CWI exam budget planner helps you add travel, code books and time away from work.

faq.q: What should a new CWI in Los Angeles learn next?
faq.a: Visual testing training to SNT-TC-1A fits naturally with welding inspection, followed by magnetic particle or ultrasonic methods if your projects call for them. See VT Level 2 training and NDT training for Los Angeles.
